articles.title: New cacao variety could help protect global chocolate supply from disease
articles.dek: Chocolate lovers may not realize it, but the future of one of the world's most popular foods is increasingly under pressure.
paragraphs: Chocolate lovers may not realize it, but the future of one of the world's most popular foods is increasingly under pressure. Diseases, shifting weather patterns and other environmental stressors are threatening cacao production globally, contributing to supply concerns and economic challenges for the millions of farmers who grow the crop that makes chocolate possible.
Now, after decades of research, Penn State scientists have developed a new disease-tolerant variety of cacao—and they say it has the potential to change the chocolate industry.

The new cacao variety builds on decades of research led by Mark Guiltinan, J. Franklin Styer Professor of Horticultural Botany and professor of plant molecular biology in the Department of Plant Sciences at Penn State's College of Agricultural Sciences, and Siela Maximova, research professor of plant biotechnology in the same department.

"For consumers, chocolate is something they expect to find on store shelves every day, but behind that product is a crop and industry facing significant challenges," Guiltinan said. "Our goal is to develop tools that help growers continue producing cacao sustainably and profitably."

Penn State's Program in the Molecular Biology of Cocoa, which Guiltinan and Maximova co-direct, traces its roots to the 1980s. Since then, researchers at the university have developed foundational tools for cacao biotechnology, mapped important genetic pathways and built one of the world's leading cacao research programs.

The university recently entered into a licensing agreement with AgroNetica, a cacao-focused biotechnology company, to work toward bringing the plant to growers worldwide. The company will advance field testing of the plants with the goal of eventually marketing the plant directly to growers, helping address some of the most significant threats facing global chocolate production.

The AgroNetica agreement represents a new chapter in the university's effort to understand and improve cacao, Maximova said, one focused on translating discoveries into technologies that can help growers, strengthen supply chains and support the future of chocolate production.

"Thanks to this long-term investment in research and maintaining a sustained program, we now have an opportunity to begin getting technologies developed here in the lab closer to the hands of farmers," Maximova said. "The focus was always on helping cacao farmers and the industry. We're now at the place where we have a partner whose expertise is moving these discoveries into real-world use."

According to Guiltinan, this new commercialization opportunity is particularly important as cacao production worldwide faces mounting threats from disease, climate variability and changing environmental conditions that jeopardize both grower livelihoods and supply chains.

Black pod disease, an especially destructive disease caused by a mold-like pathogen, alone is estimated to cause yield losses of roughly 30% worldwide, he said, while climate-related stresses continue to threaten production in major cacao-growing regions.

Native to the Amazon rainforest, cacao evolved as an understory tree growing beneath a tropical forest canopy. Today, it is cultivated across tropical regions in Africa, Asia and Latin America, often under environmental conditions that are very different from those in which the species evolved.

"Cacao evolved in a very stable rainforest environment," Guiltinan said. "It's a delicate plant in many ways. Changes in rainfall, temperature and humidity can all affect production, and some of those changes can also increase disease pressure."

Traditional cacao breeding is notoriously slow. Maximova explained that developing and evaluating new varieties can take decades because cacao trees require roughly three years to mature and produce seed. That slow rate of growth means climate change is an especially dangerous threat to its survival, she added. Not only are environmental conditions shifting faster than plants can evolve, but increased humidity and weather variability can create favorable conditions for pathogens and insect pests.
"The climate is changing faster than these trees can naturally adapt," she said. "One of our goals is to develop tools that help breeders respond more quickly to those challenges."

articles.title: Supporting children with dyslexia starts with preparing their teachers
articles.dek: A child pauses at a word, tries it, then looks to the teacher for help. Telling the word to the child can get the sentence moving.
paragraphs: A child pauses at a word, tries it, then looks to the teacher for help. Telling the word to the child can get the sentence moving. Working out what to teach so the child can read similar words independently takes a different kind of expertise.

That expertise is especially important for children with dyslexia, which involves persistent difficulties with word reading and spelling . Reading may be inaccurate, slow or effortful, and the pattern varies between children. Recognizing dyslexia is only the first step. Helping requires teaching that targets the skills involved, and that depends on teachers understanding how spoken and written language works.

Research suggests that children at risk of dyslexia benefit most from such high-quality explicit teaching. In this article, we explain what teachers need to know, what we learned from our research, and why it matters for dyslexia.

Research shows that many children with dyslexia struggle to identify or work with sounds in spoken language, which can make learning the relationships between sounds and letters harder. However, their difficulties are not all the same, and one reading attempt cannot determine what teaching they need. This is where expert knowledge matters.

Read "reach" and "react" aloud. You probably have little difficulty with either. But how would you explain why the letters "ea" make different sounds in each word? In reach, the letters work together to represent one sound, the long "e" sound. In react, the word's structure changes how we group the letters : it divides into re + act. The "e" ends the prefix re-, and the a starts act, so they represent separate vowel sounds. A prefix is a meaningful word part added at the beginning of a word. Recognizing such parts draws on morphology: knowledge of word structure.

Now consider a student who tries to read react using the "ea" sound from reach. They may be applying a familiar letter–sound relationship without recognizing where the word divides. A teacher could check whether the child can read and understand act, then build re + act and explain how the parts combine in pronunciation and meaning. The child would then practice reading the word, with later checks to see whether they could do so independently.

This is why explicit language knowledge matters. The teacher needs to understand how sounds, letters and word structure interact, then use that understanding to interpret the student's attempt and choose a useful explanation. Teachers need the knowledge and practical skill to decide what to teach next. Being able to read fluently ourselves does not automatically equip us to do that.

In our study of teachers working in the first three years of elementary school in Scotland, 122 teachers completed a knowledge assessment. Their weakest area was phonics, decoding and encoding: understanding relationships between letters and sounds and using them to read and spell. On average, they answered 53% of questions in this area correctly. This knowledge helps teachers explicitly teach word reading and spelling, two skills that dyslexia affects.

One teacher from our study captured the uncertainty: "I can identify when readers are struggling but do not yet have the right skills and experience to help them." They described "feeling deflated and like I'm failing."
The concern extends beyond Scotland. A 2026 meta-analysis of 143 studies , most conducted in English-speaking countries, identified gaps in teachers' language and literacy knowledge.

Teacher education should make this expertise an explicit part of preparation. Trainees need to understand sound–letter relationships and word structure (morphology) explicitly. They also need to learn how to assess what a child understands and decide what to teach next.

There is evidence that preparation can build this knowledge. A review of 20 studies of teacher preparation and training found that programs allowing teachers to apply their learning under expert guidance produced the largest gains in teacher knowledge. It also reported preliminary evidence of benefits for children's word reading. Knowledge development and supported practice belong together.

articles.title: AI and satellite data could give Florida earlier warnings of toxic red tides
articles.dek: Red tide, a harmful algal bloom that produces toxins, is known for causing respiratory irritation in humans and killing fish in coastal waters.
paragraphs: Red tide, a harmful algal bloom that produces toxins, is known for causing respiratory irritation in humans and killing fish in coastal waters. Recent research shows that the conversation is also shifting to include a more subtle neurological threat.

According to the Roskamp Institute, studies have linked red tide's airborne brevetoxins to brain fog, intensified migraines and cognitive fatigue, yet the public remains largely unaware of when these risks peak.

Florida State University's Bingqing Liu is a satellite oceanographer and assistant teaching professor in the Department of Earth, Ocean and Atmospheric Science. She also serves as principal investigator at the HyperCoast Lab @ FSU and uses AI and NASA satellite technology to track red tide's harmful algal blooms (HABs) in the Gulf.

Liu was part of a research team that conducted a recent study published in Scientific Reports explaining how extreme weather events, such as Hurricane Milton in 2024, can cause rapid intensification of Karenia brevis red tides. The study details how heavy rainfall and severe runoff wash large amounts of pollutants into coastal ocean waters to allow toxic algae to grow. The research reinforces the growing health risk hurricane activity poses for humans living near coastal waters.

The study also highlights the importance of using advanced hyperspectral satellite technology for monitoring HABs. For the first time, data from NASA's PACE satellite allow scientists to map and distinguish different algal groups in coastal waters, including Karenia brevis, the organism that causes Florida's toxic red tides, from other algal groups.

"New hyperspectral satellite missions such as PACE provide far more detailed information on ocean color, enabling us to distinguish phytoplankton types and not just overall abundance, including harmful species such as Karenia brevis," Liu said.

"This capability allows for earlier and more accurate detection of bloom development over large spatial scales. When combined with forecasting tools, these observations can provide advance notice of potential exposure, allowing vulnerable individuals, such as those prone to respiratory or neurological symptoms, to take precautions before conditions worsen."

While general beach reports focus on dead fish, Liu's work with hyperspectral imaging and AI offers more precise data on how these toxins move through air and water. Her research helps connect bloom detection to public health risks for Florida's coastal communities.

"AI allows us to move from simply observing harmful algal blooms to anticipating them. By combining satellite observations, such as those from NASA's PACE mission, with ocean models and environmental data, AI can identify patterns that precede red tide events, including changes in phytoplankton communities and physical–chemical conditions (e. g. , temperature, salinity, currents, and nutrient levels). This enables earlier detection and short-term forecasting, which can support timely advisories and mitigation efforts. While we cannot prevent red tide itself, we can significantly improve early warning and reduce its impacts on communities and ecosystems," says Liu.

"Red tide organisms, such as Karenia brevis, produce toxins (brevetoxins) that can affect humans in multiple ways. In coastal areas, wave action can break open algal cells and release toxins into the air, where they can be inhaled, leading to respiratory irritation and potentially neurological symptoms like headaches or brain fog. Toxins can also accumulate in shellfish, posing risks when consumed. Understanding how blooms develop, intensify and move is critical for predicting exposure pathways and protecting public health."

articles.title: Scientists uncover new way to control magnetism and topology using light in atomically thin materials
articles.dek: Envision a material whose magnetic properties and electronic topology can be toggled by exposure to light, paving the way for future electronic devices that do not rely on…
paragraphs: Envision a material whose magnetic properties and electronic topology can be toggled by exposure to light, paving the way for future electronic devices that do not rely on traditional electrical switching, which wastes energy by producing heat.

Researchers at Monash University have predicted that this kind of switching is possible in the two-dimensional magnetic topological material MnBi₂Te₄, through a type of hybrid light–matter excitation they call magnetophononic polaritons. The study is published in ACS Nano .

"Controlling magnetism and topology with light has long been a challenge in topological quantum materials research. Our calculations show a way to achieve both at once, which could enable ultrafast on–off switching of topological states," said Dr. Enamul Haque, the study's first author, who carried out the work during his Ph. D. at Monash University.

Using first-principles calculations, the researchers show that magnetophononic polaritons allow light to change both magnetic order and electronic topology. Their calculations indicate that a strong terahertz pulse, 0. 6 picoseconds long with a field of about 2 MV/cm, drives lattice vibrations that switch the magnetic coupling between the two layers of a MnBi₂Te₄ sheet 14 atomic layers thick from antiferromagnetic to ferromagnetic while the lattice is being driven (see image above).

In this state, the sheet changes from an ordinary insulator to a topological one, with protected conducting channels along its edges. The effect requires low temperatures, below about 20 to 25 kelvin, for the material to be magnetic.

In quantum materials, electrons, atomic vibrations and magnetic moments interact to produce collective excitations known as quasiparticles. Phonon polaritons are one such quasiparticle, formed when light couples to vibrations of the crystal lattice (phonons). They confine light into very small spaces, which makes them useful for nanophotonics. In MnBi₂Te₄, one of the polaritons compresses light to an effective wavelength of about 18 nanometers, compared with about 65 micrometers for light of the same energy in free space.

"What stands out in this result is that a single material can confine light tightly and also let that light control its magnetic and topological properties. Our next step is to work with experimental colleagues to test the prediction at low temperature using terahertz pulses," said professor Nikhil Medhekar, who supervised the research at Monash University.

Optically induced magnetic changes offer a route to ultrafast switching, and confined polaritons suit miniaturized photonic components. Combining both in one material points to devices in which light controls magnetic and topological electronic states, with potential uses in reconfigurable electronics, spintronics and nanophotonic switches.

Haque is currently a Postdoctoral Research Fellow at the Polytechnic University of Cartagena (UPCT) in Spain, focusing on quantum materials, condensed matter physics, and light–matter interactions, with particular emphasis on magnetic and topological phenomena. Haque investigates how fundamental quantum interactions can be harnessed to control material properties and advance future quantum and electronic technologies.

Haque is particularly interested in elucidating complex physical phenomena at the microscopic level and in developing theoretical and computational methods to study them. More broadly, Haque aims to explore fundamental questions in condensed matter physics, foster connections across research areas, and translate theoretical insights into opportunities for technological innovation.

articles.title: Extreme risk protection orders are designed to prevent gun violence. But how do they impact the people subject to them?
articles.dek: About 125 people die from gun violence through homicide or suicide in the United States every day. Many more are injured by firearms.
paragraphs: About 125 people die from gun violence through homicide or suicide in the United States every day. Many more are injured by firearms. Extreme risk protection orders (ERPOs), known in California as gun violence restraining orders, are designed to keep firearms temporarily away from people at risk of harming themselves or others.

While previous research has focused on whether these orders prevent violence, a new study from the UC Davis Centers for Violence Prevention examines a different question: What consequences—including violence prevention—do people subject to these orders attribute to them?
Detailed answers are now published in PLOS One . The paper is the first to draw directly on the experiences of people subject to ERPOs.

Researchers conducted in-depth interviews with 24 people who had been issued ERPOs in California between 2016 and 2020. The interviews, conducted from March through November 2024, were transcribed and analyzed by two researchers to identify common themes and important differences in participants' experiences.
Participants reported a wide range of consequences after being issued an ERPO:
The findings illustrate that respondents' experiences are not uniform. This suggests that evaluations of ERPO laws should consider a broader range of outcomes in addition to violence prevention.

"To comprehensively evaluate extreme risk protection orders, researchers and policymakers must consider their full range of consequences, including those reported by respondents themselves," said first author Veronica Pear. Pear is a researcher at the Centers for Violence Prevention and an assistant professor in the UC Davis Department of Emergency Medicine. "This broader evidence can guide policy refinements that preserve these laws' public safety benefits while reducing avoidable harms."

The researchers caution that the study reflects participants' own accounts and cannot determine whether the ERPO itself caused the outcomes they described. They also caution that the study included only 24 respondents and is not representative of ERPO respondents generally.
However, they note the interviews provide important insight into perceived consequences that may not be captured in administrative data or measures typically used to evaluate ERPO outcomes.

" Extreme risk protection orders are intended to prevent tragic outcomes, and research suggests they can reduce suicide risk," said Garen Wintemute, senior author of the study. Wintemute is an emergency room physician and director of the UC Davis Centers for Violence Prevention. "As these laws continue to evolve, listening to respondents can help policymakers identify practical improvements in implementation while maintaining the goal of preventing violence."

articles.title: Potential antimalarial compound discovered in institute's microbe collection
articles.dek: Scientists hunting for a new malaria treatment may have found a solution within a historical natural compound collection housed at The Herbert Wertheim UF Scripps Institute…
paragraphs: Scientists hunting for a new malaria treatment may have found a solution within a historical natural compound collection housed at The Herbert Wertheim UF Scripps Institute for Biomedical Innovation & Technology.

Globally, malaria remains one of the most widespread and deadly infectious diseases, sickening an estimated 280 million people annually. It disproportionately kills small children, with about 600,000 deaths every year. Spread through biting mosquitoes in tropical areas, malaria parasites are growing resistant to standard therapies such as chloroquine and artemisinin .

"The parasites are evolving, so it's critically important to identify new antimalarial drugs that have mechanisms of action that differ from past drugs," said chemist Ben Shen, Ph. D. , founder of the Natural Products Discovery Center at The Wertheim UF Scripps Institute. "The compounds we identified originated in soil microbes and extracts housed within our natural products collection."
The team discovered several compounds capable of rapidly killing the malaria parasite at all stages of its life cycle, unlike existing antimalarial drugs, Shen said.

Co-first author Chantal Bader, Ph. D. , a postdoctoral researcher in Shen's lab, said the team used a systematic process to find the best candidates from a subset of the 122,550-strain collection, seeking compounds that had not been studied before.

"Bacterial extracts contain thousands of different metabolites. The challenge is to find an active extract, to identify which specific metabolites in these complex mixtures are responsible for the activity, and then to confirm they are truly novel," Bader said.

The researchers started their quest by screening 81 purified natural compounds selected from the institute's collection. Their target was a drug-resistant malaria parasite known to cause severe disease. That step revealed six promising candidates from five chemical families.

Then they expanded their screening to 1,531 samples created by 425 microbes, a group of bacteria called Actinobacteria. Of those, they found about 20% had antimalarial properties. Filtering out those toxic to humans, they then studied the top candidates' chemical composition and activity. That revealed several compounds that had not previously been studied by scientists.

The researchers then cultured the bacteria that produced the novel compounds. They optimized their production, characterized their chemical structures and named them SPAs, short for sphaeriaurantins. The SPAs come from a rare and little-studied group of soil bacteria called Sphaerisporangium, Shen explained.

Testing showed the best of the SPAs cleared 99. 9% of the multidrug-resistant malaria parasite, Plasmodium falciparum , from blood and cultured liver cells, meaning the compound worked at multiple stages of the parasite's life cycle. Their testing indicated that the SPAs are unlikely to develop drug resistance.
Their research was published in August in the Journal of the American Chemical Society .

The path from lead discovery to approved medicine can take many years. The researchers' next steps involve characterizing the pharmacological and therapeutic potential of the SPA scaffold, Shen said. That will require identifying and validating its primary molecular target and understanding the mechanism of action, he said.

The Natural Products Discovery Center at The Wertheim UF Scripps Institute consists of microbes, their extracts and partially purified samples. Shen and his research team have been painstakingly studying the collection to build a genome database for the world's scientists to search for new natural products.

articles.title: NASA Invites Media to Crew Completion of Yearlong Mars Simulation
articles.dek: The four volunteers who lived and worked in a simulated NASA Mars mission for more than a year will exit their habitat on Saturday, Oct.
paragraphs: The four volunteers who lived and worked in a simulated NASA Mars mission for more than a year will exit their habitat on Saturday, Oct. 31, after 378 days of isolation in a facility at the agency’s Johnson Space Center in Houston. Health and performance data collected from the simulation can help NASA develop methods to counter human spaceflight risks for future Artemis and Moon Base missions.

Beginning at 3 p. m. EDT, NASA will provide live coverage of the volunteers’ departure from the Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog (CHAPEA, pronounced cha-pea’-ah) mission habitat. The exit ceremony will be streamed on NASA Johnson’s YouTube and social accounts.

Johnson Center Director Vanessa Wyche and NASA astronaut Jack Hathaway will provide remarks. The CHAPEA crew members Ross Elder, Ellen Ellis, James Spicer, and Matthew Montgomery also will provide remarks.

Media are invited to watch the CHAPEA Mission 2 ceremony live at NASA Johnson on a screen outside the hangar holding the CHAPEA facility, after which a subject matter expert will be available in person to answer questions. Media will have the opportunity to capture the moment the crew exits the building, stepping outside for the first time in more than a year.

U. S. media interested in attending the activities in person, or media interested in speaking virtually with the CHAPEA Mission 2 crew members in the days following completion of their mission, must contact the NASA Johnson newsroom no later than 2 p. m. , Friday, Oct. 30, at jsc-newsroom@mail. nasa. gov .

The second CHAPEA mission began on Oct. 19, 2025. Four crew members have lived and worked inside a 3D-printed 1,700-square-foot facility, simulating Mars mission operations, conducting simulated spacewalks, exercising, performing habitat maintenance, growing plants, and more, while operating under stressors that future deep space crews will likely experience. These included communication delays, resource limitations, and isolation.

Data from the mission can aid preparation for NASA’s lunar missions by optimizing food system design, efficient use of crew time, bandwidth on NASA’s Deep Space Network , and other aspects of living in deep space. In addition, data can help flight doctors and psychologists strengthen spaceflight medical care and behavioral support practices to ensure crew readiness and performance.

articles.title: The Ocean’s Mysterious “Snow” Could Be Hiding a Powerful Climate Secret
articles.dek: A surprising property of the tiny particles sinking through the ocean could help determine how much carbon is stored in the deep sea.
paragraphs: A surprising property of the tiny particles sinking through the ocean could help determine how much carbon is stored in the deep sea. Scientists have discovered that the stickiness of marine snow affects how easily bacteria can break it down, potentially changing how much carbon reaches the ocean depths.

Researchers at UC San Diego’s Scripps Institution of Oceanography and the University of Lincoln found that particularly gooey marine snow resists bacterial degradation. Their findings, published October 8 in Science , suggest that highly viscous particles can transport more than six times as much carbon to the deep ocean as less viscous particles.

Marine snow consists of tiny clumps of dead plankton, waste, mucus, minerals, and other debris that continuously descend through the water column. As these particles sink, they carry carbon from the sunlit surface ocean toward deeper waters, where some of it can remain stored for hundreds or thousands of years.

Scientists estimate that marine snow transports more than 10 gigatons (11 billion U. S. tons) of carbon away from the surface each year. However, only about 2 gigatons (2. 2 billion U. S. tons) reach depths where the carbon can remain stored for extended periods. Much of the sinking material is broken down or recycled before reaching those depths.

The new research identifies particle viscosity, a measure of resistance to flow, as an important factor in this process. Marine snow particles vary in composition and consistency, and those differences influence how bacteria colonize and consume them.
Understanding these interactions required a technique that had previously been unavailable: directly observing individual living bacteria as they navigate the microscopic structure of mucus.

“Observing individual bacteria interacting with the physical structure of mucus had never been possible,” said Bryce Inman, who began investigating the problem in 2021 while working as a postdoctoral scholar at Scripps Oceanography.

After four years of unsuccessful attempts, Inman and his colleagues, including Scripps microbiologist and professor emeritus Farooq Azam, developed a working approach in 2025. By combining 3D confocal microscopy with specialized fluorescent molecules, they could map the intricate physical structure of marine snow and track how bacteria interacted with it. The imaging technique is described in a companion study published in Nature Communications .

The images showed that bacteria colonize less viscous regions near the surface of marine snow particles more easily than the thicker, more resistant material inside. These internal regions present a physical barrier that bacteria must gradually break down before penetrating farther into the particle.

“Bacteria can latch on to less viscous portions of each particle, but cannot reach more viscous regions until they break it down,” Inman explained. “Think of it like a worm in an apple: the flesh is easy to penetrate, but the core is tough to chew through”

Laboratory experiments confirmed that more viscous marine snow takes longer for bacteria to degrade and fragment. Computer simulations further suggested that these resistant particles can sink to greater depths before breaking apart. Together, the findings indicate that viscosity can substantially influence how much carbon escapes recycling in shallower waters and reaches the deep ocean.

The newly developed imaging method could also help researchers investigate interactions between bacteria and mucus in other environments. Similar relationships occur in coral reefs, kelp forests, plant root systems, and the digestive tracts of humans and other animals.

“Mucus, slime, whatever you want to call it, has a surprising amount of structure,” Inman said. “There are bulges, crevasses, all this sort of structure to it that we really had no idea about at a scale smaller than bacteria. This is the first time we’re really examining this physical habitat.”

By making these microscopic environments visible, the technique could support research into how bacteria colonize mucus, interact with its physical structure, and influence processes ranging from ocean carbon storage to coral reef recovery and human health.

articles.title: Aging’s “Zombie Cell” Problem May Have a Solution, Scientists Discover
articles.dek: “Zombie cells” become harder to clear with age, and a new study reveals why the immune system struggles to remove them.
paragraphs: “Zombie cells” become harder to clear with age, and a new study reveals why the immune system struggles to remove them.

Researchers at Albert Einstein College of Medicine have identified a breakdown in protein recycling that helps explain why senescent cells, often called “zombie cells,” accumulate in aging tissues. In experiments involving older mice, restoring that process reduced senescent-cell buildup, inflammation, and tissue scarring. The findings, published in Nature Aging , suggest a possible way to help the immune system clear these cells more effectively.

Senescent cells remain alive after they stop dividing, but their activity changes. Although they can support tissue repair, their prolonged presence can fuel chronic inflammation and age-related disease. Most of the new experiments involved mice, with human lung samples providing evidence that the biological changes may also occur in people.

“In older animals, age-related changes in both senescent cells and the immune cells responsible for removing them allow these zombie cells to accumulate and play a role in disease,” said study leader Ana Maria Cuervo, M. D. , Ph. D. “By restoring cellular recycling, we may be able to help the body’s own defenses clear these cells more effectively.”
Some injured cells enter senescence and release substances that recruit other cells to support repair. Once that work is done, immune cells called macrophages normally remove the senescent cells.

Macrophages also fight infection, dispose of dead cells, and regulate inflammation and tissue repair. The researchers found that their ability to remove senescent cells depends partly on chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA), a recycling process that uses specialized “chaperone” molecules to select damaged or unnecessary proteins for breakdown.

When the team genetically altered mice so their macrophages lacked CMA, senescent cells lingered at wound sites, and healing slowed compared with control animals. The experiment showed how a defect inside immune cells can turn a temporary repair response into a lingering obstacle to recovery.

Cuervo, a leading CMA researcher, is a distinguished professor of developmental & molecular biology and medicine, the Robert and Renee Belfer Chair for the Study of Neurodegenerative Diseases, and co-director of Einstein’s Institute for Geroscience. Her earlier research established that CMA declines with age. Subsequent work linked the resulting buildup of cellular waste to Alzheimer’s and other neurodegenerative diseases, as well as atherosclerosis and diabetes.

The age-related decline in CMA also affects senescent cells themselves. To examine this, the researchers collected fibroblasts, cells found in connective tissue, from young and old mice. They then used drugs to stop the cells from dividing and induce senescence in the laboratory.

Cells from young mice responded by increasing CMA activity. Cells from old mice failed to increase their already low activity, allowing certain proteins to escape proper breakdown. They consequently released harmful substances that encouraged neighboring healthy cells to become senescent and interfered with macrophages’ ability to recognize and remove them.

At the same time, macrophages from older animals had lower CMA activity than those from younger animals and were less able to engulf senescent cells. Aging therefore disrupted both the cells awaiting removal and the immune cells responsible for clearing them.

Age-related changes in senescent cells could affect drug development. Researchers are developing senolytics to eliminate these cells, but testing them on cells taken from young animals and induced to become senescent in the lab may not accurately predict their effects in older bodies.

The findings pointed toward another possibility: improve cellular recycling so senescent cells release fewer harmful substances and macrophages can recognize and engulf them more effectively. The team tested a compound it had previously developed, a small-molecule CMA activator called CA77. 1.
Aged mice given CA77. 1 orally every day for five months accumulated fewer senescent cells in several organs. They also showed fewer signs of inflammation and fibrosis, the buildup of scar tissue.

articles.title: Earwax is both slippery and sticky – this weird combo might lead to safer insect repellents
articles.dek: Here’s a bit of a riddle for you: What has the consistency of both toothpaste and dough, can absorb twice its weight in water and still remain sticky, was used by medieval…
paragraphs: Here’s a bit of a riddle for you: What has the consistency of both toothpaste and dough, can absorb twice its weight in water and still remain sticky, was used by medieval artists as a binder in paint and has been hypothesized by physicians to repel insects?

The medical term for earwax is cerumen, based on keros, the Greek word for beeswax. People have been pondering earwax since ancient times. Ancient hygiene kits including picks and spoons to remove earwax have been found in archaeological sites worldwide .

Even today, it remains a perpetual question: to remove or not to remove your earwax? The answer: Don’t do it . The general medical belief is that ears are self-cleaning , and earwax brings benefits such as lubricating the ear canal, fighting infection and acting like a sticky net to trap debris before it reaches the eardrum. By poking in there you can accidentally make matters worse, pushing wax deeper or scratching your delicate ear canal.

Cerumen impaction – or blocked earwax – affects about a fifth of the American population , leading to 12 million patient visits per year. Blockages are worsened by daily activities such as wearing earbuds or hearing aids.

Another common problem with ears is wedged debris. For children, much of this is self-inflicted, in the form of items such as Legos or erasers. But for many adults who have something stuck in their ear, the debris is insects, such as ants, beetles, flies or cockroaches.

While rare for the average person, insects in the ear occurred with such frequency over the years that physicians began to wonder whether earwax evolved as a natural barrier for insects. But how would such a barrier work?

To answer this question, my Ph. D. student David Ancalle led experiments with earwax and insects. We teamed up with Yuhang Hu and her student Donjing He , experts in the behavior of soft solids such as hydrogels. As mechanical engineers, we wanted to focus on the physics rather than the chemistry of earwax.
Our research , published in the journal Soft Matter, shows that earwax can, in fact, stop insects without the use of dangerous chemicals.
To do experiments, we needed voluminous amounts of earwax.

Initially we obtained earwax from deceased mammals such as pigs, sheep and rabbits. Eventually we turned to our friends and family. A person has only a grain of rice’s worth of earwax in each ear. Due to a mutation in a single gene , East Asians have dry, flaky earwax, while people of African or European descent have wet, squishy earwax .

To simulate an ant climbing into an ear canal, we used a glass beaker with its rim coated in earwax. Ants, like many insects, are climbing specialists, capable of traveling across many kinds of surfaces. To climb rough surfaces, ants have spikes on their feet , like mountain climbers do, that helps them grasp onto ridges and cracks. For smooth surfaces, ants unfurl wet suction cups , which can support 60 times their body weight on smooth glass.
Watching ants trying to climb earwax showed us how strange a substance it really is. Rough earwax slowed them down, but with their claws they made progress.
But as soon as ants tried to climb smooth earwax, they fell immediately.
From these experiments, we concluded that earwax had anti-stick properties when in contact with the insects’ feet.

We next conducted experiments with ants crawling through an earwax-coated tunnel, more similar in size to a human ear canal. As the ants attempted to travel through the tunnel, earwax stuck to them. Once coated, they groomed furiously, unwilling to walk until they had removed as much as possible. Even after several minutes of effort, the ants still had earwax sticking to hard-to-reach places.

So, earwax is a paradoxical material: It is simultaneously slippery, thanks to the lipids it contains, but also sticky. Similar to many materials – including ketchup, paint and shampoo – it thins out when it is physically deformed, what physicists call shear-thinning.

The dual qualities of earwax have to do with its unique composition. Earwax is made up of flakes of skin cells held together with a binder. This blend forms a kind of sponge with microscopic holes. When a body overproduces earwax, it heaps up in boulders that ants can easily climb over.

When the substance is smooth, however, ants rely on their wet suction cups. The holes in the earwax absorb the drops produced by the ants, preventing them from attaching. Absorbency makes earwax fundamentally different from commonly used forms of pest control.

In your local store, you will find sticky surfaces such as fly paper or chemicals that kill the insects. Some researchers look to nature to find bio-friendly alternatives to using chemicals; for example, plants have properties that prevent insects from climbing .
From this study, we learned that the ear is also a model for insect repellency. Earwax is made of natural materials but has a structure that prevents ants from sticking to it.

The porosity of earwax also gives it unique properties. We showed it can absorb twice its weight in water yet still cling to the walls of the ear. This water-absorbing ability may help prevent water from accumulating on the delicate eardrum and fend off infections such as swimmer’s ear .
Scientists don’t yet understand the complex relationship between earwax, water and bacteria. Some studies show that earwax kills bacteria , but other studies find that earwax harbors bacteria .

Our experiments showed that earwax is most challenging to insects when similar to the thin layer of earwax maintained by a healthy human body. Wax would accumulate more in human ears if not for two self-cleaning mechanisms. The skin in the ear canal grows outward like a conveyor belt. Over 8-10 weeks, this process – called epithelial migration – pushes the oldest earwax out of the ear.

Simultaneously, earwax dries over time, transforming from a gooey state to a brittle one that readily cracks. Every time you talk or chew , your ear canal deforms , and physicians found that this movement helps to dislodge the drier, older earwax.

articles.title: Unexpected Discovery of Abnormal Antibodies Could Help Explain Childhood Cancer
articles.dek: Laboratory experiments show that antibodies associated with childhood cancer can enter cells and bind DNA repair proteins, suggesting a possible route by which the immune…
paragraphs: Laboratory experiments show that antibodies associated with childhood cancer can enter cells and bind DNA repair proteins, suggesting a possible route by which the immune system could weaken genetic safeguards.

Years before some children were diagnosed with cancer, their blood already contained antibodies directed against proteins that normally repair damaged DNA. Researchers in Norway have found that these antibodies were much more common among children who later developed cancer than among those who did not, raising the possibility that the immune system itself may interfere with a cell’s ability to protect its genetic material.

Childhood cancers, including leukemia, myeloma, neuroblastoma, and osteosarcoma, differ from adult cancers in their causes, locations, and responses to treatment. Children have had far less time to accumulate DNA damage from environmental exposures, lifestyle factors, and aging. Their tumors therefore tend to contain fewer mutations and often arise from immature cells, such as stem cells or progenitor cells that can develop into more specialized cell types.

Cells rely on hundreds of proteins to identify and repair damage or errors in their DNA. The Norwegian researchers suspect that this protective machinery may sometimes be disrupted by auto-antibodies, antibodies that mistakenly target the body’s own proteins rather than foreign threats. If these antibodies interfere with DNA repair, genetic damage could accumulate even without inherited defects in the genes responsible for maintaining the genome.

To investigate this possibility, Serguienko, Dr Ola Myklebost, and their colleagues analyzed the proteome, or collection of expressed proteins, in tumor and blood samples from 175 adults and children with sarcoma or acute lymphoblastic leukemia. The samples were collected between 2014 and 2017 through the NoSarC Norwegian Sarcoma Study, the Norwegian Childhood Cancer Biobank, and the Oslo University Hospital Cancer Research Biobank. The team compared them with samples from anonymized healthy individuals, including blood donors, children participating in the Bergen Growth Study, and children visiting a clinic in Bergen.

Children with cancer between the ages of two and 19 had substantially more circulating IgG antibodies targeting DNA repair proteins than young adults or older individuals. These antibodies primarily recognized proteins associated with six genes: RAD52, NUMA1, ALKBH7, APBB1, UNG, and MGMT. Although these genes are closely involved in DNA repair, they were not significantly mutated in the cancers studied. This raised the possibility that the proteins could be disrupted by the immune system even when the genes encoding them remained largely intact.

Finding these antibodies in children who already had cancer, however, could not establish whether they appeared before the disease or developed in response to it. The researchers therefore examined blood samples collected years earlier from 59 school-age children who participated in two long-term British studies, the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children and Born in Bradford.

Roughly half of these children subsequently developed cancer before turning 30, while the others did not. Comparing the two groups allowed the researchers to investigate whether antibodies targeting DNA repair proteins were present before cancer was diagnosed.

“Although this cohort is small, it was the best we could find internationally,” said Myklebost, an emeritus professor of molecular oncology at the University of Bergen. “Even so, we were able to show that indeed, children who later got cancer (on average six years after blood sampling) were about eight times more likely than their healthy peers to have antibodies to at least one core antigen involved in DNA repair.”

The findings, published in Frontiers in Immunology , suggest that these antibodies can appear well before cancer develops. Their presence alone does not establish that they cause the disease, however. To explore whether they might actually interfere with DNA repair, the scientists conducted additional experiments using living cells.

Those experiments showed that the auto-antibodies could enter cells, particularly during the stage when cells finish growing and prepare to divide. Once inside, the antibodies appeared to concentrate around a cellular structure called the TIGER organelle, where transcription factors and other short-lived but essential proteins are produced and modified.

“We showed that many children with various types of cancer have antibodies against some of their own DNA repair proteins. We also demonstrated that such ‘auto-antibodies’ can enter live cells and bind to – and probably inhibit – the activity of these essential proteins,” said corresponding author Myklebost.

articles.title: Scientists Discover a Surprising Dental Benefit of Cranberry Juice
articles.dek: In a small human study, unsweetened pure cranberry juice was linked to slower plaque regrowth and lower acid production, hinting at a possible oral health benefit.
paragraphs: In a small human study, unsweetened pure cranberry juice was linked to slower plaque regrowth and lower acid production, hinting at a possible oral health benefit.

Cranberry juice has a reputation for being tart, acidic, and often sugary, qualities that might seem poorly suited to protecting teeth. A small human study from the University of Illinois Chicago, however, found that unsweetened pure cranberry juice was associated with slower dental plaque regrowth and lower acid production.

UIC College of Dentistry researcher Christine Wu examined whether compounds naturally found in cranberries could affect dental plaque bacteria, which feed on sugars and produce acids that contribute to enamel decay. Cranberries contain proanthocyanidins, anti-inflammatory compounds known for their ability to interfere with the attachment of bacteria such as E. coli to cells.
“Just like sugar damage is linked to diet, I’m interested in how the food and beverages we consume can help combat the harmful bacteria and benefit our oral health,” Wu said.

Rather than testing isolated cranberry compounds in the laboratory, Wu and her colleagues used commercially available beverages. Fourteen children and eight adults were randomly assigned to drink either unsweetened pure 100% cranberry juice, a cranberry juice cocktail containing 27% juice with added sugar, or water.

“It was important to us to conduct these tests with human participants and use products available on the market. Most cranberry juice studies have been conducted using laboratory-prepared cranberry juice extract. Moreover, limited studies have been performed in children,” said Wu, who is a professor of pediatric dentistry.

Participants arrived on the morning of the study with plaque that had accumulated overnight. Researchers first used cotton swabs to collect plaque samples from one side of each participant’s mouth. After rinsing with water, participants drank three small portions of their assigned beverage, swishing each several times before swallowing.
Thirty minutes later, researchers collected plaque from teeth that had not been swabbed earlier. This allowed them to compare plaque collected before and after exposure to the beverages.

Plaque exposed to pure cranberry juice appeared to regrow more slowly than the samples collected before the experiment. Swishing with pure cranberry juice was also associated with lower acid production in both children and adults. That matters because acids produced by plaque bacteria can contribute to the breakdown of tooth enamel.

The findings raised the possibility that cranberry juice could eventually be considered a “functional beverage” with potential oral health benefits. Wu noted that other commonly consumed juices, including orange and apple juice, had not shown the same promise in her work.

“Most people think of cranberry juice as very sour, very acidic and sugary, and therefore may not contribute positively to oral health. This study found the opposite: that cranberry juice affected dental plaque regrowth and acid production, which may counteract some of the damage done by sugar,” she said.

The results are preliminary. The study included only 22 participants and measured short-term effects, so additional experiments will be needed to determine whether the findings hold up in larger groups and over longer periods.
For now, Wu said she would not rule out occasionally using pure cranberry juice as a mouth cleanser.
“But maybe by adding an appropriate sugar substitute,” she said, “to make it a bit more palatable.”

articles.title: Scientists Discover That Eating Peanuts Every Day May Help Protect the Aging Brain
articles.dek: A daily serving of peanuts may improve insulin sensitivity in the aging brain, potentially supporting memory.
paragraphs: A daily serving of peanuts may improve insulin sensitivity in the aging brain, potentially supporting memory.

Peanuts may offer more than a convenient source of protein and healthy fats. New research suggests that eating them regularly could help the aging brain respond more effectively to insulin, a hormone that plays an important role in memory, learning, and communication between nerve cells. As people grow older, the brain can become less sensitive to insulin, a change linked to age-related cognitive decline.

In a small clinical trial, researchers at Maastricht University Medical Center in the Netherlands found that eating unsalted, skin-roasted peanuts daily for 16 weeks improved insulin responsiveness in brain regions involved in memory. The study, conducted by the Institute of Nutrition and Translational Research in Metabolism (NUTRIM), was published in Food & Function .

“The hormone insulin plays an important role in the brain, where it supports memory and other cognitive processes. As people age, the brain may become less responsive to insulin, which has been linked to age-related cognitive decline,” says Dr. Peter Joris, the study’s senior author and an associate professor in the Department of Nutrition and Movement Sciences at NUTRIM, Maastricht University Medical Center.

The trial included 31 healthy adults aged 60 to 75. Each participant completed a 16-week period of eating peanuts and a control period without them. This randomized, controlled crossover design allowed researchers to compare each person’s results under both conditions.

During the peanut period, participants ate 60 grams (approximately two servings), or about 2. 1 ounces, daily. Premeasured packets helped them follow the prescribed amount, which they could eat in one sitting, divide throughout the day, or add to meals. They were instructed to consume the peanuts in the morning or afternoon.

The changes in insulin responsiveness appeared in a cluster on the brain’s right side, encompassing parts of the lingual gyrus, hippocampus, parahippocampal gyrus, and posterior cingulate gyrus. These regions are involved in memory.

To assess the brain’s response, researchers administered insulin through the nose and measured the resulting changes in regional cerebral blood flow (CBF). They used arterial spin labeling magnetic resonance imaging (ASL-MRI), combining advanced imaging with a controlled dietary intervention lasting several months.

Earlier results from the 16-week peanut intervention, published in 2025 in Clinical Nutrition , showed a 3. 6% increase in global cerebral blood flow, which supplies the brain with oxygen and nutrients, alongside a 5. 8% improvement in verbal memory.
The team also assessed cognitive performance using the Cambridge Neuropsychological Test Automated Battery (CANTAB) and measured intrahepatic lipid (IHL) content, or liver fat, with abdominal MRI.

“Our study found that daily peanut consumption beneficially affected insulin responsiveness in memory-related brain regions in older adults,” says Dr. Peter Joris, the study’s senior author and an associate professor at Maastricht University Medical Center. “These findings suggest that enhanced regional brain insulin responsiveness may contribute to the cognitive benefits of unsalted, skin-roasted peanut intake.”

“Multiple nutrients present in peanuts, including unsaturated fats, dietary fiber, vitamins and minerals, and bioactive phytochemicals, could potentially contribute to the observed brain benefits,” adds Joris. “Peanuts are also a good source of plant-based protein and are especially rich in L-arginine. L-arginine is a key precursor of nitric oxide (NO), which has been reported to facilitate learning and memory performance.”

The NUTRIM study was supported by funding from The Peanut Institute Foundation. The funder did not have a role in the study design, implementation, analysis, or interpretation of the data or the writing of the manuscript.

articles.title: School librarians are vanishing from Michigan schools just when they are needed most
articles.dek: Fewer than 10% of Michigan public schools report having a school library staffed with a trained school librarian.
paragraphs: Fewer than 10% of Michigan public schools report having a school library staffed with a trained school librarian.

Although Michigan strongly recommends that schools employ certified librarians , the state does not require them. In the 2023–24 school year, the state ranked 46th in the student-to-librarian ratio , with one school librarian for every 2,760 students.

The lack of school librarians impacts students across Michigan, but particularly in low-income communities like Detroit and Flint and more isolated ones like Alcona County in the northern Lower Peninsula and Ontonagon in the Upper Peninsula, exacerbating disparities in resources for young people.

We are scholars in library and information sciences from Wayne State University , studying information access and ethics and equity in education and school libraries . Currently, we are conducting a statewide campaign to contact every school in Michigan and learn about their libraries, staffing, book collections, technology resources and more.

Michigan’s 2025–26 School Aid budget funded our statewide survey to measure the school librarian shortage and guide efforts to address it. Our work, and the work of many others, reveals how school librarians help students become strong readers and informed citizens.

A missing librarian is harder to see than an empty bookshelf. A room full of books can look like a school library. But if students cannot borrow those books, teachers have no librarian to plan lessons with, and no one leads author visits or digital citizenship lessons, the space offers only a fraction of what a school library can provide.

School librarians bring those services to life. Also called school library media specialists, they hold a teaching certificate and complete advanced education . They connect students with books they want to read and work with teachers to build richer lessons, using library resources to extend learning beyond the textbook.

Their impact stretches far beyond standardized test scores, though studies link strong library programs with higher student achievement and improved student literacy , especially for struggling readers . They can instill a love of reading and teach technological skills , which is critical in the age of artificial intelligence.

At our Michigan School Census symposium held in 2026, Michigan school librarians and a principal described what that work looks like. Brian Peck, a teacher librarian at Detroit’s UPrep Academy, helped students research and build a library where none had existed. He reported that 334 students voluntarily visited and checked out books during the previous school year.

At West Ottawa, librarian Julia Reynolds described replacing crowded shelves with displays that let children see book covers. Circulation quadrupled, she reported. A principal on the panel explained how district support helped schools make library visits a priority from the first week of school.
Access to information is only a start. Students also need help making sense of what reaches them through searches, social media and AI.
AI can create convincing fake videos of students doing or saying things they never did, harming their reputations and undermining trust in what people see online.

Less visible forces shape students’ information worlds, too. Algorithms and online platforms often dictate which search results and suggested videos appear first. Students need to understand that the first result is not necessarily the most credible or trustworthy source. AI is becoming so prominent that even elementary school students are learning about it.
Information literacy means knowing how to find, judge and use information. School librarians turn those skills into practice.
For a history assignment, a librarian might help students compare a newspaper account with a firsthand record. Who produced each source? What might explain their different accounts?
The same habits apply to AI. Students can trace a claim to its source, check whether the source exists and compare what it says with the generated answer. A confident response still needs evidence.

Guided by certified school librarians, students can build upon these foundations and learn to effectively find, evaluate and use information, including news articles about a historic event for a social studies assignment or to analyze current social media trends. Students can also judge the accuracy, recency and relevance of information. They learn to apply information in decision-making, writing and other forms of communication.
Knowing whether information is trustworthy is an important skill. Deciding what to do with it is another.
Digital citizenship includes deciding whether to post someone’s photo, seeking their permission before doing so, and choosing not to share a fake video.
Recent research emphasizes that digital citizenship prepares students to be empowered online and act ethically, safely and legally in digital environments.
Our work also starts with the knowledge young people bring to school.

Project Restoring Urban School Libraries helped classroom teachers earn the additional endorsement needed to become school librarians. The program combined mentoring with coursework that drew on students’ cultures, including using hip-hop to explore how young people find, create and share information.
Students start by examining the media they already use. A lesson might ask them to trace a sample, credit its creator and discuss what changes when someone else’s work reaches a new audience.

Principal preparation programs can help school leaders understand what school librarians contribute beyond book checkout. But principals and school librarians often train in separate academic units: colleges of education and schools of library and information science. Without shared coursework or joint projects, principals may complete their training without learning how to work with a school librarian.

articles.title: We studied 1,584 data centers – and found the buildings full of machines are tied to modest local job growth
articles.dek: Data centers require enormous investments : land, buildings, computer equipment and power infrastructure.
paragraphs: Data centers require enormous investments : land, buildings, computer equipment and power infrastructure. Yet, once they’re up and running, they tend to employ no more than a few dozen people in occupations such as IT technicians, engineers and security guards. With billions of dollars flowing into new data centers across the United States, communities are asking what they will get in return .

Skepticism about the local benefits of data centers is contributing to growing opposition to their construction , from Ohio to Texas . That pushback contributed to delays or cancellations of US$156 billion in proposed data center projects in 2025 alone.

We are professors who study real estate and urban economics , including how large place-based investments shape local economies. So we set out to answer a question at the center of these fights: Do data centers actually create jobs where they are built?

To find out, we teamed up with four colleagues to study what happens to local employment after data centers open. We found that new data centers that opened from 2000-2023 created 1,000 to 1,300 jobs in the counties where they are located, on average. But those jobs, which are for work performed outside data centers rather than inside them, take a few years to appear. They are mostly in industries that support data centers, not in restaurants or shops.
Data centers can create jobs in at least three ways beyond employing people who work inside them.
First, they can increase demand for local suppliers, from security companies that protect the facilities to electrical contractors that maintain their equipment.
Second, data center employees and workers at these suppliers may spend more money locally, supporting restaurants, stores and other local services.

Third, companies already operating data centers may expand their facilities, while other operators may decide to build nearby. Once a location has the electricity, fiber connections and other infrastructure needed to operate a data center, further investment may become easier.

We assembled detailed information on 1,584 U. S. data centers that opened between 2000 and 2023. For each facility, we recorded its location, opening date and power capacity, which is a standard way to compare facilities of different sizes. We then matched these records with federal data on employment, wages and the number of businesses in each county.

Isolating the effect of data centers isn’t straightforward. Operators don’t choose locations randomly. They look for reliable electricity, fiber connections, available land and friendly local regulations. Those places may already be growing, so new jobs might have appeared even without a data center.

To account for this, we tracked employment in counties that received data centers – such as Loudoun County in Virginia, Berkeley County in South Carolina, Morrow County in Oregon, and others – before and after the operation of the facility began. We then compared those trends with similar counties that did not receive data centers. We also looked at whether larger facilities brought bigger job gains.

During the first two years after a county’s first data center opened, we found little change in employment outside construction. After that, jobs begin to grow. Three to five years after a center opened, we found that these counties had roughly 1,000 to 1,300 additional nonconstruction jobs than comparable counties without data centers.
Bigger investments brought bigger employment gains. Five years after new data center capacity is installed, each additional megawatt is associated with about 7. 4 more nonconstruction local jobs.

Part of that gain, however, reflects further expansion. Each megawatt installed is associated with another 1. 7 megawatts of capacity over the following years. Once that later growth is counted, our estimates work out to about 2. 7 nonconstruction jobs per megawatt of eventual data center capacity. A large 100-megawatt facility, for example, would be correlated with roughly 275 additional local jobs outside the data center itself.
The types of jobs created help explain what is happening.

Employment gains are concentrated in transportation and warehousing, professional and technical services and real estate. These industries may serve or benefit directly from data centers or from the investment and infrastructure they bring.
By contrast, we found little evidence of job growth in restaurants, stores and other local services.

We also found that more data center investment tends to follow in the same county. Most often, the companies already operating in a county expand their facilities. Other companies generally don’t move into that same area to build new data centers.

Our study has limits. It covers data centers that opened through 2023, before the current wave of massive facilities were built to power AI. Larger data centers do not necessarily create proportionally more jobs, so our findings may not apply to today’s biggest projects.

We also looked only at job gains and did not explore whether data centers are worth their cost to local communities. These facilities consume large amounts of electricity and water, can generate noise and may receive substantial tax breaks from local and state governments. We did not address any of those concerns.

Our findings do show that data centers can create jobs beyond the small number of people working inside their walls. But that does not mean every one of them is a good deal for their local community. And whether those additional jobs justify the costs remains an open question.

Lyndsey Rolheiser receives funding from the Canadian Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) and the Real Estate Research Institute (RERI).

articles.title: Leave home with a plan: What to pack in your medical kit and when to seek care for symptoms abroad
articles.dek: When people prepare to see a doctor before an international trip, vaccines usually dominate the conversation.
paragraphs: When people prepare to see a doctor before an international trip, vaccines usually dominate the conversation.

And while vaccines are important, many of the health problems most likely to derail a trip cannot be prevented with a vaccine: Diarrhea, respiratory infections, motion sickness and flare-ups of existing medical conditions are all common – and none of them can be headed off with a shot.

The U. S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates that between 43% and 79% of travelers to low- and middle-income countries become ill during or after their trip, although most of those illnesses are mild.
As an infectious diseases physician who specializes in travel and tropical medicine, I counsel many patients before they leave the country and care for them when they come home sick.

A good pretravel visit to the doctor should end with more than a list of shots. You should know which illnesses you could encounter on your itinerary, which symptoms you can reasonably handle yourself, which medicines to carry and how to use them, and which warning signs mean it is time to find a doctor.

Infectious disease risks abroad are constantly shifting. A good healthcare provider who specializes in travel and geographic medicine keeps up with these developments so that the advice you get reflects what is happening now, not last year.
Since early 2025, South America has seen new yellow fever outbreaks that redrew long-standing risk maps and an unusual hantavirus cluster that spread from person to person aboard a cruise ship .

Cases of dengue fever worldwide roughly doubled in a single year , and another tropical disease – chikungunya – also flared in new places, including the largest outbreak ever recorded in China . Fiji declared a fast-growing HIV outbreak . And common respiratory viruses, from influenza to COVID-19, continue to circulate all over the world.

In my own clinical research with colleagues, we have seen travelers who returned to the U. S. with serious – and occasionally fatal – infections, such as malaria and hepatitis , often after dangerous delays in recognizing what was wrong.
Travel health advice is not one-size-fits-all. A week at a Caribbean resort, a safari in East Africa and a month trekking in Nepal carry very different risks.

Even the likely cause of a fever changes with the destination. Dengue is a leading concern after travel in much of Latin America and Asia, while malaria is especially important in parts of sub-Saharan Africa, and typhoid and paratyphoid fever loom largest in South Asia.
What you do matters, too – freshwater swimming, visiting caves, animal contact, hiking and staying in remote areas each add their own hazards .

So bring your actual itinerary to the appointment. Tell your doctor not just which countries you’ll visit, but whether you’ll be in cities or the countryside, what you plan to do, how high you’ll go, how long you’ll stay and how easily you could reach a reliable hospital.

For minor illnesses, you can plan to treat yourself. Travelers’ diarrhea is the best example of such an illness. Depending on the destination and season, it affects an estimated 10% to 40% of travelers during the first two weeks of a trip. Most cases clear up on their own within a few days, but having a plan makes a real difference.

Ask your doctor what to do if diarrhea develops. Oral rehydration salts help replace fluids when losses are heavy. Loperamide , an over-the-counter antidiarrheal, can reduce how often and how urgently you need a bathroom, but it should not be used on its own when diarrhea comes with a fever or blood in the stool. Depending on your destination and medical history, your doctor may also give you an antibiotic to carry and use only for moderate or severe diarrhea.

When it comes to treatments you’ll be administering yourself, it’s as important to ask your doctor when to use each medicine as it is to have the drugs on hand. Antibiotics have side effects, can leave you carrying drug-resistant bacteria and contribute to antibiotic resistance worldwide – so they are best saved for the episodes that truly need them.

The same logic applies to other predictable problems. Someone prone to seasickness on a planned boat trip might discuss meclizine or a scopolamine patch . A traveler flying straight into a high-altitude city such as Cusco, Peru, or La Paz, Bolivia, might discuss acetazolamide, a prescription medicine that helps the body acclimatize and roughly halves the risk of altitude sickness during rapid ascents.

A basic travel health kit keeps a small problem from becoming a big one. The contents depend on the traveler and the trip, but useful items include pain and fever medicine, bandages, antiseptic, oral rehydration salts , loperamide , antihistamine and anything prescribed specifically for the trip.

People with chronic conditions should pack enough of their regular medications for the entire trip, plus extra in case of delays. Keep medicines in their original labeled containers, carry them in your hand luggage rather than checked bags, and consider bringing a copy of your prescriptions written with the drugs’ generic names.

Replacing a medication abroad can be harder than you expect. Drugs may have different names, formulations or availability in other countries, and counterfeit or low-quality medicines remain a real problem in some places. Some medications that are routine in the U. S. are restricted or banned elsewhere. Insulin, injectable drugs, controlled substances and anything that needs refrigeration will require extra planning.

Travel medicine is full of remedies with better reputations than evidence. Ginger is often recommended for motion sickness, but studies have produced mixed results . Acupressure wristbands for motion sickness do not outperform placebos . And despite their popularity, probiotics are not recommended for preventing travelers’ diarrhea , as their efficacy is still unknown.

Coca leaves and coca tea are widely used for altitude symptoms in the Andes, but there is no strong evidence that they prevent altitude illness – and the same is true of garlic, ginkgo and vitamin E. “ Natural” does not mean effective , or even harmless, particularly when a supplement interacts with a prescription drug .
Perhaps the most important part of any plan is recognizing when self-care is no longer appropriate.

Seek medical attention for severe dehydration, persistent vomiting, difficulty breathing, confusion, severe abdominal pain or an illness that is rapidly getting worse. Bloody diarrhea or diarrhea with a significant fever calls for medical care rather than simply taking an antidiarrheal and carrying on with your trip.

articles.title: How should AI be regulated? Follow the harm
articles.dek: As artificial intelligence technologies grow ever more powerful, so do the risks they pose and with them the urgency of regulating AI.
paragraphs: As artificial intelligence technologies grow ever more powerful, so do the risks they pose and with them the urgency of regulating AI.

In July 2026, OpenAI’s advanced models hacked into AI company Hugging Face’s systems during internal cybersecurity evaluations by communicating through unauthorized channels and working around safeguards developers had imposed on the models. In January 2026, Google and Character. ai, which makes a role-playing AI chatbot, agreed to settle a wrongful death lawsuit brought by Megan Garcia. Her 14-year-old son, who used the chatbot heavily, died by suicide.
As these and other cases show, AI harms can emerge across different technologies, organizations and contexts. As a legal scholar focused on AI and digital harms , I study how to regulate AI.

Policymakers and industry commentators have tended to frame regulation as a trade-off between the risks of AI and the risks of regulating AI. In its 2025 AI Action Plan , the Trump administration called for removing “red tape and onerous regulation,” which it said hinders economic growth. The administration has also sought to limit conflicting state AI laws.

In contrast to the broad concerns about the costs of AI regulation, AI harms have largely been addressed through rules specific to particular technologies. The federal Take It Down Act, signed in 2025, for example, addresses nonconsensual intimate imagery , including AI-generated deepfakes, as do various state laws . These approaches are crucial, but they don’t solve the problem by themselves.

The emerging patchwork of rules has yet to establish a regulatory architecture that connects protected interests, institutional obligations and individual rights across AI technologies. Protected interests are rights recognized by the law, such as property ownership and personal privacy. A harm-centered approach would begin with those interests and use them to shape legal obligations that span relevant systems, organizations and people.
A harm-centered approach starts by identifying the fundamental interests that AI systems can threaten. These overlapping interests include:
These examples are not exhaustive. Other interests may also be at stake as AI technologies evolve.

The same interest can be threatened by different technologies and different entities. A teenager’s safety can be harmed by the engagement mechanisms of a social media platform or by an AI companion designed to sustain an emotional relationship.

Designing regulations based on a concept of harm allows laws and principles to follow problems as the technology changes. And it helps determine obligations imposed on developers, deployers and other stakeholders involved in AI.

For instance, AI developers could be required to conduct harm assessments throughout the development of AI systems, identifying reasonably foreseeable harms, documenting how they tested for them and explaining what mitigation measures they took. Companies or government agencies that deploy AI systems could also have duties to monitor harms after deployment. Serious or recurring harms could trigger obligations to report them to relevant regulators, affected individuals or the public, depending on the nature and severity of the harm.

A harm-centered framework could also recognize corresponding rights for people affected by AI systems, including rights to notice and opportunities to seek redress where appropriate. These rights would arise from the same protected interests that justify obligations on companies.

The point is to build a regulatory architecture on the detection and reduction of harm across AI applications, developers and users. What matters most is whether and how AI-enabled design or operation contribute to harm.

Environmental law, for instance, has long regulated industries by focusing on their environmental effects rather than on technology alone. It requires regulated companies to monitor emissions and discharges, maintain records and report specified releases to regulators . Some reporting requirements also make information available to the public. Environmental review under the National Environmental Policy Act requires federal agencies to assess environmental effects and provides opportunities for public participation.
AI governance could draw on this logic, determining who is responsible for assessment, monitoring, disclosure and mitigation based on types of harm.

A harm-based focus would not eliminate technology-specific rules. Some technologies create distinctive risks that justify targeted rules, such as disclosure requirements for AI-generated deepfakes or safeguards for AI systems used in high-stakes decisions. And focusing on harm does not mean regulating every conceivable risk of harm.

But I believe that harm should become the organizing principle of AI regulation. New AI systems will bring harms policymakers have not yet anticipated. The challenge is to build a framework for the harms we know, as well as the harms we do not yet know.
