articles.title: Viruses obey the laws of physics – studying how can help researchers understand why they infect people differently and lead to better treatments
articles.dek: The beauty of physics at the cellular scale is part of what draws biomedical engineers and biologists like us to the field of mechanobiology : the study of how physical…
paragraphs: The beauty of physics at the cellular scale is part of what draws biomedical engineers and biologists like us to the field of mechanobiology : the study of how physical forces influence biology.

Physics holds relevance everywhere . You can see physics at work on how the cells lining your veins and arteries feel the flow of your blood, the cells of your spinal discs carry the weight of the vertebrae surrounding them, and the cells of your lung cyclically stretch with every breath.

If each and every building block of the body experiences some combination of these physical forces, then the viruses that infect them must contend with a variation of those forces, too. How viruses interact with these forces affects how well they can infect cells and cause severe illness.
When microscopic virus particles enter the body, they rely upon the mechanical machinery of the cells they infect to continue their life cycle.

Many viruses will first latch onto receptors on the cell’s surface. Movement of the cell’s membrane – driven by its internal cytoskeleton – will bend and wrap around the invading particle, pinching off a tiny bubble that carries it inside. In this process of endocytosis , the cell swallows the virus.

Once inside, the virus is shuttled along the cell’s internal scaffolding. It releases its genetic material and hijacks the cell’s machinery to make copies of itself. New virus particles will then exit the cell to infect its neighbors.

Each of these steps is physical at its core. The tautness of a cell’s membrane could make it easier or harder to wrap around a virus. The cytoskeleton that transports these virus particles is the same lining that cells use to sense and push against their surroundings . What’s more, the stiffness of a cell’s environment will shape how the cell spreads and organizes itself , which may change how susceptible it is to an invader.

A healthy individual often can quickly recover from an infection. However, for someone with a preexisting condition such as pulmonary fibrosis – where the tissue of the lungs has stiffened and can no longer stretch to full capacity – a viral infection may make their condition worse.
This mechanical predisposition of tissues to infection is one reason health professionals urge the public when sick to avoid the elderly and immunocompromised.

Our laboratory looks into the mechanobiology of different types of tissues to understand how the physical forces people endure in daily life can worsen disease. Repetitive lifting and loading can wear down the discs of the spine , for example, and mechanical ventilators can overstretch and injure lungs .

But growing cells in a plastic petri dish – the standard method in most virology labs – shows only part of the story. Tissue culture plastic is significantly stiffer than living tissues , closer to a countertop than a lung. Cells notice the difference during experiments; the stiffness of their surroundings can change both how they behave and how they respond to an infection.

To bring the mechanics of the human body into the lab, we grow lung cells on thin layers of a flexible, silicone-based polymer called PDMS that we fine-tuned to match the softness of actual lung tissue. These sheets sit in small chambers that will cyclically stretch and relax on command from a computer that sets how far and how long they stretch. This allows us to mimic the physical movements of breathing.
We can use a virus engineered to make infected cells glow red under a microscope to monitor how it spreads among cells. But how can we monitor how the mechanics of a cell change during infection?

Our team follows the activity of two important proteins, YAP and TAZ , that act as the cell’s force sensors. When a tissue experiences stiffness or tension, these sensors will move into the nucleus and turn on genes tied to growth and repair. When those forces are lacking, as is generally the case in softer tissue, YAP and TAZ remain inactive and stay put outside of the nucleus.

Some viruses are known to tap into this same signaling pathway , so examining YAP and TAZ may offer a window into whether mechanical forces and infection influence one another. Using the gene-editing tool CRISPR , we can attach a fluorescent tag onto YAP or TAZ and watch their activation in real time under a microscope as they react not only to mechanical forces but potentially to infection as well.

With this platform, we can better answer questions such as whether lung cells will respond to infection differently under different forces or whether these forces will change how well viruses infect. Thus far, our early findings suggest that the stiffness of a cell’s environment affects how heavily cells become infected: Lung cells grown on stiffer, fibrosis-like surfaces appear to become more heavily infected.

Understanding the mechanics of viral infection is of particular interest to researchers and clinicians, given the persistent prevalence of respiratory infections worldwide. The common cold, COVID-19 and the flu represent merely a drop in the viral infection bucket: More than 200 species of virus are known to infect humans.

Mechanobiology may be just as important to the cycle of infection as its biochemical or immunological aspects. Under a microscope, the differences are clear between a stiff, overworked lung and a soft, healthy lung, and viruses may navigate these environments in adaptive ways.

As scientists map these mechanical signals, new possibilities for preventing and treating infection are opening up. Among them are therapies that could reduce the physical strain on tissues or even biomarkers that could tell patients whether they are susceptible to tissue stiffening or certain infection paths and the possible damage they may cause.
The human body is just as mechanical as it is chemical, and so, too, are the infections it encounters.

articles.title: From 54% to 100%: Scientists Reveal a Potential Breakthrough in Quantum Technology
articles.dek: Scientists have proposed a surprisingly simple way to improve photon absorption using specially engineered waveguides, potentially making future quantum technologies far more…
paragraphs: Scientists have proposed a surprisingly simple way to improve photon absorption using specially engineered waveguides, potentially making future quantum technologies far more efficient.

Quantum technologies depend on a process that remains surprisingly unreliable: transferring a single photon between two quantum bits, or qubits. With conventional methods, the receiving qubit successfully absorbs the photon only about 54 percent of the time. This inefficiency creates a major obstacle for quantum computers, secure quantum communication, and future quantum networks.

Researchers at TU Wien have proposed a way to overcome this limitation by changing the shape of a photon’s wave as it travels between qubits. Their calculations and computer simulations suggest that the method could achieve 100 percent absorption under ideal conditions.

Two qubits (two atoms, for example) can exchange quantum information when one emits a photon and the other absorbs it. But photons do not behave simply like tiny particles moving between two points. Their wave properties determine how efficiently they can be transferred.

“When a qubit emits a photon, you must not picture the photon as a tiny particle that is simply shot out,” says Dr. Zeyu Kuang from the Institute of Theoretical Physics at TU Wien. “The photon is a wave, and a wave has a certain shape and a certain extension.”

The researchers compare photon emission to striking a bell. The sound begins strongly and gradually fades, much like the wave emitted by a qubit. Unfortunately, this waveform is poorly suited to absorption by another qubit. A pulse that gradually increases in strength before reaching its peak would work much better.

The solution relies on time-reversal symmetry, a fundamental principle of quantum mechanics. Under ideal conditions, a quantum process can run in reverse, meaning a photon emitted with a particular waveform can be perfectly absorbed if that waveform is reversed in time.

“This follows from time-reversal symmetry in quantum mechanics,” Oliver Diekmann explains. “Under ideal conditions, quantum dynamics are reversible. If a qubit perfectly emits a photon with a particular waveform, the time-reversed process tells us which waveform that qubit can absorb perfectly.”

To achieve this reversal, the researchers propose using a specially engineered optical waveguide. Unlike light traveling through a vacuum, different frequency components of light inside a waveguide can move at different speeds. This behavior, known as dispersion, can be controlled to reshape the photon pulse during transmission.

By adjusting the waveguide’s dispersion, the team calculated that an emitted photon could arrive at the receiving qubit with precisely the waveform needed for optimal absorption. Under ideal conditions, the theoretical success rate could reach 100 percent.

“We calculated how this goal can be achieved and simulated the process on a computer,” says Prof. Carlos Gonzalez-Ballestero. “Our results indicate that the required setup should be technically feasible. This passive approach could significantly improve the absorption of photons by qubits and thereby increase the efficiency of many quantum technologies.”

Although the approach has not yet been demonstrated experimentally, the simulations suggest that carefully designed waveguides could make photon transfer substantially more reliable, potentially improving the performance of future quantum computers and communication networks.

articles.title: How a Johnson Mentor Shapes the Next Generation of NASA Talent
articles.dek: When Rice University student Malvika Bhardwaj asked her mentor Daniel Cohen, a Guidance, Navigation & Control (GN&C) engineer at NASA’s Johnson Space Center, whether he had…
paragraphs: When Rice University student Malvika Bhardwaj asked her mentor Daniel Cohen, a Guidance, Navigation & Control (GN&C) engineer at NASA’s Johnson Space Center, whether he had time to keep teaching interns with his busy workload, he answered, “You decide what’s important.”
In honor of National Mentoring Day on Oct. 27, Bhardwaj reflects on how Cohen’s advice and support has shaped her internship experience at Johnson.

Through NASA’s Office of STEM Engagement , interns like Bhardwaj contribute to agency projects while learning from NASA mentors and gaining technical skills and hand-on experience to build a future career in space exploration.

Bhardwaj studies computational and applied mathematics at Rice University and interns with the GN&C team, which focuses on how spacecraft determine their position and maneuver in orbit. She is developing tools to analyze thruster firings on the U. S. Deorbit Vehicle that will help NASA safely deorbit the International Space Station at the end of its operational life. Bhardwaj also uses computer simulations to test the vehicle’s control system and identify conditions under which it could fail.

“I’ve learned about the culture of community and support at Johnson and NASA as a whole. Daniel made an effort to introduce me to the team and include me in conversations and meetings. I saw how team members step up to help one another and keep the whole unit moving forward,” Bhardwaj said.

Cohen, a Rice University alumnus with a master’s in mechanical engineering, began his NASA career as a flight operations intern in 2020. He later held internships in docking dynamics, propulsion systems, and GN&C analysis before joining Johnson as a full-time engineer in August 2024.

His current work includes developing simulations and models for studies of the U. S. Deorbit Vehicle, analyzing its control algorithms and GN&C performance, and evaluating SpaceX’s design at multiple life-cycle reviews.
He also analyzes settings for the Orion spacecraft’s docking camera, which provides positioning measurements that can help inform navigation during future Artemis rendezvous activities.

Cohen supports Bhardwaj beyond her internship, giving her a closer look at how colleagues collaborate on projects and share ideas. He sets aside a couple of hours each week to teach interns topics such as orbital mechanics and control systems.

Bhardwaj took Cohen’s advice to heart: How she spends her time and energy reflects what she values. She believes that her internship has shown her that problem-solving is rarely an individual effort. Team members bring different perspectives and need to understand how their work connects to a larger project.

Working alongside interns in outreach, social media, and digital design has also broadened Bhardwaj’s view of STEM careers. “No matter what interests you, there’s likely a role for you here,” she said.
She was proud to complete her first project, a set of analysis tools she built from scratch. Working through the debugging process and seeing a finished, functioning product was especially rewarding.
Bhardwaj’s advice to students interested in NASA internships is to apply even if they do not feel fully prepared.
“You’re probably never going to feel 100% ready, but so much of the learning happens on the job,” she said. “Trust in your ability to navigate new environments.”

articles.title: A-81 Reaches South Georgia
articles.dek: Some Antarctic icebergs linger close to home for decades, running aground near the ice shelves that spawned them or circling partway around the continent on coastal currents.…
paragraphs: Some Antarctic icebergs linger close to home for decades, running aground near the ice shelves that spawned them or circling partway around the continent on coastal currents. Others, like Iceberg A-81, make a faster exit, heading north out of the Weddell Sea along a route well-traveled by the region’s bergs.

Fast is relative, though. After breaking from the Brunt Ice Shelf in January 2023, the roughly 1,550-square-kilometer (600-square-mile) berg spent more than three years in the Weddell Sea, carried along the coast by the clockwise-flowing Weddell Gyre. By May 2026, it reached the tip of the Antarctic Peninsula. It then moved north into the Scotia Sea, and by late October 2026, it approached the remote island of South Georgia in the South Atlantic Ocean, 2,300 kilometers (1,400 miles) north-northwest of the Brunt Ice Shelf.

This image, acquired by the MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) on NASA’s Terra satellite, shows the berg on October 20. In the days before, its progress slowed noticeably, and it appeared to be bumping along the edge of the island’s underwater shelf, according to Jan Lieser of Australia’s Bureau of Meteorology and Christopher Shuman of the University of Maryland (retired). South Georgia has slowed and even stopped icebergs before. In 2025, for instance, Iceberg A-23A ran aground on the shelf and later broke apart .

Though Iceberg A-81 was a steadfast traveler once it broke free, it took its time in becoming an iceberg in the first place. For about 35 years, one of the Brunt Ice Shelf’s rifts known as Chasm 1 was relatively stable. Then, around 2012, it began growing again, and by 2019, it was advancing quickly enough that a break seemed imminent . But the floating glacial ice held on for several more years until finally, in January 2023, the berg let go .

Calving is a normal part of the life cycle of ice shelves, but scientists keep a close eye on Brunt, which has recently shed several large icebergs in quick succession and is home to the British Antarctic Survey’s Halley Research Station , a major base for Earth, atmospheric, and space science research since the 1950s. Besides A-81, the ice shelf calved Iceberg A-74 from the North Rift in 2021 and Iceberg A-83 from the Halloween Crack in 2024. A-74 has since broken up, while A-83 remains intact and is trailing A-81 northward, along with a handful of other icebergs that appear to be clearing out of the Weddell Sea.

articles.title: NASA’s Perseverance Offers Clues to Protect Crews From Mars Dust
articles.dek: Over 1,645 Martian days, NASA’s Perseverance Mars rover measured the fine and ultrafine Martian dust particles found clinging to samples of spacesuit materials that are…
paragraphs: Over 1,645 Martian days, NASA’s Perseverance Mars rover measured the fine and ultrafine Martian dust particles found clinging to samples of spacesuit materials that are carried aboard the rover, including some that are small enough to penetrate the lungs and enter the bloodstream. The findings will be published Tuesday, Oct. 27, in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences and could inform spacesuit and habitat design, dust-removal procedures, and crew health standards for future NASA missions to Mars.

“NASA has a long history of turning challenges into workable solutions and of finding creative ways to use the data that we have to answer questions beyond what it was originally collected for,” said Lindsay Hays, acting director, Planetary Science Division, NASA Headquarters in Washington. “Dust has been a surface-exploration challenge since the Apollo program. Perseverance is giving our engineers and flight surgeons measurements they can use to improve our existing designs well before the first American astronauts arrive on Mars.”
Lunar dust scratched visors, degraded outer spacesuit layers, and damaged their seals during NASA’s Apollo missions, and some crew members reported symptoms similar to hay fever.

Rounded by wind-driven collisions with other particles, dust grains on Mars are less abrasive than those on the Moon. They also are enriched in sulfur, chlorine, and iron and contain more silica than lunar dust. Regional and global dust storms on Mars can keep the grains recirculating throughout the atmosphere as well.

The rover carries a set of five samples of spacesuit material. The swatches , each three-quarters of an inch (20 millimeters) square, are part of a calibration target used to test the settings of SHERLOC (Scanning Habitable Environments with Raman and Luminescence for Organics and Chemicals), an instrument on Perseverance’s robotic arm. The calibration target for another instrument that provided the dust measurements, called PIXL (Planetary Instrument for X-ray Lithochemistry), carries a sample of Teflon and of basaltic glass.
Because Teflon contains no elements that PIXL can directly detect, whatever elemental signals the X-ray spectrometer picks up from that sample comes from dust resting on it.

The team also analyzed swatches of Teflon and Vectran, two materials used in spacesuits, on SHERLOC’s calibration target. NASA sent the swatches to Mars to study how spacesuit materials hold up on the planet’s surface.

“Perseverance’s main job is to search for signs of ancient microbial life, but the mission was also designed to help prepare for human explorers. That effort includes technology demonstrations like MOXIE (Mars Oxygen In-Situ Resource Utilization Experiment) and Ingenuity , as well as the spacesuit samples,” said Katie Stack Morgan, Perseverance’s project scientist at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California.

While earlier measurements on Mars resolved dust particles down to about 3 micrometers across, PIXL detected two categories of even smaller particles: fine particles measuring less than 2. 5 micrometers (a human hair is about 70 micrometers wide) and ultrafine particles around 100 nanometers (about 700 times thinner than a human hair). Particles on PIXL’s Teflon target and SHERLOC’s Vectran swatch averaged about 2 micrometers. On PIXL’s basaltic glass and SHERLOC’s Teflon swatch, dust particle sizes ranged down to about 100 to 300 nanometers.

Static electricity appears to determine which size dust particles stick to which surface. Dust grains become charged as they collide in the air, and different materials on the calibration target attract grains of different sizes. The finest particles stayed attached through years of driving and drilling. Organic polymers like SHERLOC’s Teflon spacesuit sample are common in the outer layers of spacesuits, and the results show they readily collect fine dust.

The study also found that some materials hold less dust than others, which could guide future choices of materials and protective coatings for spacesuits and habitats. Designs such as suitports , which let astronauts enter a suit attached to the outside of a habitat, and dual-chamber airlocks could reduce how much dust gets inside astronauts’ living quarters.

“NASA has a long history of turning challenges into workable solutions and of finding creative ways to use the data that we have to answer questions beyond what it was originally collected for,” said Lindsay Hays, acting director, Planetary Science Division, NASA Headquarters in Washington. “Dust has been a surface-exploration challenge since the Apollo program. Perseverance is giving our engineers and flight surgeons measurements they can use to improve our existing designs well before the first American astronauts arrive on Mars.”
Lunar dust scratched visors, degraded outer spacesuit layers, and damaged their seals during NASA’s Apollo missions, and some crew members reported symptoms similar to hay fever.

Rounded by wind-driven collisions with other particles, dust grains on Mars are less abrasive than those on the Moon. They also are enriched in sulfur, chlorine, and iron and contain more silica than lunar dust. Regional and global dust storms on Mars can keep the grains recirculating throughout the atmosphere as well.

The rover carries a set of five samples of spacesuit material. The swatches , each three-quarters of an inch (20 millimeters) square, are part of a calibration target used to test the settings of SHERLOC (Scanning Habitable Environments with Raman and Luminescence for Organics and Chemicals), an instrument on Perseverance’s robotic arm. The calibration target for another instrument that provided the dust measurements, called PIXL (Planetary Instrument for X-ray Lithochemistry), carries a sample of Teflon and of basaltic glass.
Because Teflon contains no elements that PIXL can directly detect, whatever elemental signals the X-ray spectrometer picks up from that sample comes from dust resting on it.

The team also analyzed swatches of Teflon and Vectran, two materials used in spacesuits, on SHERLOC’s calibration target. NASA sent the swatches to Mars to study how spacesuit materials hold up on the planet’s surface.

“Perseverance’s main job is to search for signs of ancient microbial life, but the mission was also designed to help prepare for human explorers. That effort includes technology demonstrations like MOXIE (Mars Oxygen In-Situ Resource Utilization Experiment) and Ingenuity , as well as the spacesuit samples,” said Katie Stack Morgan, Perseverance’s project scientist at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California.

While earlier measurements on Mars resolved dust particles down to about 3 micrometers across, PIXL detected two categories of even smaller particles: fine particles measuring less than 2. 5 micrometers (a human hair is about 70 micrometers wide) and ultrafine particles around 100 nanometers (about 700 times thinner than a human hair). Particles on PIXL’s Teflon target and SHERLOC’s Vectran swatch averaged about 2 micrometers. On PIXL’s basaltic glass and SHERLOC’s Teflon swatch, dust particle sizes ranged down to about 100 to 300 nanometers.

Static electricity appears to determine which size dust particles stick to which surface. Dust grains become charged as they collide in the air, and different materials on the calibration target attract grains of different sizes. The finest particles stayed attached through years of driving and drilling. Organic polymers like SHERLOC’s Teflon spacesuit sample are common in the outer layers of spacesuits, and the results show they readily collect fine dust.

The study also found that some materials hold less dust than others, which could guide future choices of materials and protective coatings for spacesuits and habitats. Designs such as suitports , which let astronauts enter a suit attached to the outside of a habitat, and dual-chamber airlocks could reduce how much dust gets inside astronauts’ living quarters.

articles.title: NEO Surveyor’s Sunshade Gets Inspected
articles.dek: The large sunshade of NASA’s Near-Earth Object (NEO) Surveyor is mounted on an assembly ring during inspections in a clean room at BAE Systems Space & Mission Systems in…
paragraphs: The large sunshade of NASA’s Near-Earth Object (NEO) Surveyor is mounted on an assembly ring during inspections in a clean room at BAE Systems Space & Mission Systems in Boulder, Colorado, in July 2026.

The sunshade structure stands 20 feet (6 meters) tall and measures 8 feet (2. 4 meters) wide at its base. Its two flat panels, joined at a 23. 5-degree angle, were covered with 864 interconnected solar cells and then tested before arriving in Colorado. This specialized solar array can produce up to 2 kilowatts of power and will generate all the required electricity to charge the onboard batteries that power the spacecraft’s systems.

Built by Applied Aerospace in Stockton, California, the sunshade structure was outfitted with its solar cells by SolAero Technologies in Albuquerque, New Mexico, in January. Environmental testing of the sunshade and solar array was completed at a commercial thermal vacuum testing facility in El Segundo, California, in March and it was delivered to BAE Systems Space & Mission Systems ahead of schedule in May.

When in space, NEO Surveyor will seek out some of the hardest-to-find asteroids and comets, some of which may be located in the direction of the Sun — a region of sky where ground-based optical telescopes have a harder time searching.
